Kegan presented a sequence of six evolutionary balances: incorporative, impulsive, imperial, interpersonal, institutional, and interindividual.

The object (O) of each balance is the subject (S) of the preceding balance. Kegan uses the term subject to refer to things that people are "subject to" (embedded in; current stage’s episodes) but not necessarily consciously aware of. He uses the term "object" to refer to things that people are aware of and can take control of (what they can reflect on; the previous stage’s episodes).

Siegler’s "overlapping waves" framework (now broadly supported) shows children using multiple strategies in parallel, with frequencies shifting over time, not flipping stage switches. Meanwhile, inhibition, working memory, and shifting improve protractedly into adolescence and beyond, scaffolding many "Piagetian" achievements as continuous growth in control rather than sudden structural reorganization.

During each cognitive/behavioral phase transition, multiple strategies (e.g similarity-based vs rule-based categorization) will coexist, with the better strategy gradually winning as it sees better outcomes. During each phase transition, new strategies are usually discovered through imitation, but can also be discovered through open-ended search/simulation.

Quinian Bootstrapping: How Representations Become More than the Sum of their Parts

Enrichment (most learning; gathering facts/tuning weights within a current theory) vs. Conceptual Change (restructuring the graph of concepts itself)

AGI Application: Your architecture needs two distinct optimization loops.

Inner Loop: Gradient descent/Hebbian updates (Enrichment).

Outer Loop: Symbolic Program Induction (Conceptual Change). You cannot reach AGI solely by "enriching" a pre-training loss curve; the agent must periodically "refactor" its internal code to support higher abstractions.

The Algorithm of Bootstrapping

1. Placeholder Symbols: The agent learns a set of symbols (e.g., the count list "one, two, three...") without knowing their meaning. They are computationally "empty" placeholders stored in long-term memory. 2. Structural Alignment: The agent learns the relations between these placeholders (e.g., "two comes after one") and aligns this structure with an innate core system (e.g., aligning the count list with the "parallel individuation" system for tracking objects). 3. Inductive Leap (The "Snap"): The agent realizes the isomorphism between the two structures. The placeholder "Two" is mapped to the concept of "a set of 2." Crucially, the agent induces a new rule (the successor function: N+1N+1) that transcends the core system, allowing them to represent any integer, far beyond the innate limit of 3 or 4. Does this also happen during the transition from concrete to formal operations (class logic to propositional logic)?

The Centrality of Play

Childhood as a solution to explore-exploit tensions

The role of play objects and object play in human cognitive evolution and innovation.

Children aged 1-5 years allocate between a quarter to a third of their time to object play, such as stacking and sorting blocks and cups 9, 10

Active inference: "Play" is re-interpreted not as random behavior, but as epistemic foraging-actions taken specifically to resolve uncertainty and minimize "surprise" (prediction error). Recent studies have successfully modeled infant behavior using these principles, showing that children will choose actions that maximize "information gain" rather than just reward. This is a massive shift from Behaviorist (reward-based) models to Constructivist (prediction-based) models.

Heavy reliance on Shulz’s work here

Play-based learning is the mandated pedagogy in early years’ curricula in many countries (Hirsh-Pasek et al., 2009; Pyle et al., 2017) and is regarded as developmentally appropriate practice (Copple and Bredenkamp, 2009). Researchers have widely agreed that play can be characterized as a voluntary, intrinsically motivated, child-directed, and process- rather than goal-oriented behavior that contains elements of choice (Rubin et al., 1983; Pellegrini, 2013; Weisberg et al., 2013; Trawick-Smith, 2015; Daubert et al., 2018).

Zosh et al. (2018) define play as a spectrum that allows for different types of play, ranging from free play as voluntary, intrinsically motivated, and process-oriented behavior directed by the child to more goal-oriented and adult-directed forms of playful instruction. In between these two poles, guided play represents a blend of free play and playful instruction (Zosh et al., 2018). Guided play can be described as a playful activity that is directed by the child, i.e., the child is autonomous to decide what to do, for how long and at what pace. The adult’s role in guided play is to prepare a play environment and support the children’s activities to facilitate learning (Weisberg et al., 2013, 2016; Zosh et al., 2018).

Guided play shares strong commonalities with the guided inquiry principle, which has been identified as one of the most effective approaches to learning and teaching (Mayer, 2004; Alfieri et al., 2011; Lazonder and Kamp, 2012). Researchers have frequently framed guidance in inquiry-based science teaching within the scaffolding construct (Hmelo-Silver et al., 2007). In the scaffolding literature, both material scaffolds and an adult’s verbal scaffolds are considered effective in guiding children’s learning (van de Pol et al., 2010; Martin et al., 2019). Accordingly, guided play can take at least two different forms (Weisberg et al., 2016), guided play with material scaffolds only, and guided play with additional verbal scaffolds.

Curriculum Learning is Fractal in Time and Scale

Evolution follows a curriculum of its own; phylogenesis (species evolution), sociocultural history (the cultural evolution of tools and signs), ontogenesis (individual development), and microgenesis (moment-to-moment unfolding during problem-solving)

Metalogical knowledge

Monitoring, evaluating, and understanding the logical structure of arguments, distinct from merely performing the reasoning itself. While standard reasoning involves solving a problem (e.g., "If A then B..."), metalogical reasoning involves checking if that solution was valid, identifying why it was valid, and distinguishing the structure of the argument from its content.

A child may correctly answer a logic puzzle (implicit logic), but only an adult can explain why the answer must be true regardless of the specific words used (explicit metalogic).

Children acquire ever more explicit knowledge regarding logical categories such as inference, consistency, indeterminacy, necessity, and validity as well as proof tactics or strategies such as reductio ad absurdum, systematic generation of possible states of affairs consistent with the premises, and a search for counterexamples. Increasing metalogical knowledge, in turn, brings greater control over the inference process by way of the intentional use of explicit logical categories as norms or constraints on thinking (Moshman 1990, 1998, 2004, 2013b).

D. Moshman’s theory of metacognition places metacognition at the center of reasoning development

He splits the metalogical system into two sections (procedural and explicit):

Strategies: knowledge of and control over logical procedures, like "search for counterexamples" or "reductio ad absurdum" (more procedural)

Understanding: representations of uncertainty given premises, evidence, and conclusions + distinctions of types of inference (more explicit)

Broader points

Development involves a self-reflective process by which elements implicit in intellectual acts are rendered explicit and, as such, come under conscious, intentional control, thereby becoming applicable across a wider set of circumstances. This is an internal process, though it is supported by specific types of social interaction (Moshman, 1998, 2004).

Preschool and early school-age children are able to make a variety of deductive inferences that comply with logical norms, but in Moshman’s view these inferences do not represent reasoning because they are not consciously or purposefully constrained by particular inferential norms. Conclusions as the outcomes of inferential acts are not conclusions per se for the young child, but simply facts, in principle indistinguishable from observational facts. Moshman, however, considers some knowledge of inference and of inferential form and norms to be implicit in children’s thinking at this stage (Moshman, 2013b). During the middle childhood years, these implicit elements are rendered increasingly explicit as reflective processes generate metarepresentations of them decoupled from the contexts of their use, and as they become coordinated with other relatively explicit aspects of metalogical knowledge.

The development of metalogical knowledge and its association with success on deductive-reasoning paradigms is well understood at this point and has been documented extensively by Moshman (1998, 2004, 2013a).

A "self" is essentially a unified utility function. Without a stable conception of self (personality/values), an agent cannot have consistent long-term goals. It might solve a math problem brilliantly one minute (Intelligence) and then delete its own operating system the next because it lacked a value hierarchy (Irrationality).

Must possess a recursive self-symbol that allows it to predict how its own mental states (confidence, confusion, planning) interact with that physical world; this is an abstract prediction problem over cognitive processes themselves.

The will to power

Exploring something when there is relevance, uncertainty/error, and an actual hypothesis as to the causal structure. Missing any of these will lead to no learning taking place (i.e no relevance -> no attention; no uncertainty/error -> no uncertainty/error (or no perception of it) -> no learning/attention; no priors -> discounted as noise or as fear-/escape-worthy)

Levels of personal epistemology

Greater sophistication in informal reasoning goals and skills is associated with a relatively more constructivist and evaluativist personal epistemology (Kuhn, 1991; Kuhn & Franklin, 2006).

Levels of personal epistemology (Kuhn)

1. Absolutist view, where knowledge is an objective packet of facts located outside the self, usually held by experts. If you believe this, "reasoning" is just retrieval; there is no need to argue, only to find the correct answer. 2. The second is the Multiplist view, where one realizes experts disagree, so knowledge becomes purely subjective. In this phase, "reasoning" is irrelevant because all opinions are equal valid personal possessions. Many plateau here. 3. Evaluativist view. This is the understanding that while knowledge is constructed by human minds (constructivist) and includes uncertainty, not all opinions are equal. Some claims are more valid than others based on the weight of evidence and the coherence of the argument. The quote states that people who hold this specific worldview demonstrate significantly greater sophistication in "informal reasoning"-the ability to create arguments, cite evidence, and, crucially, generate and refute counter-arguments.

Reflective judgment model (stages of assumptions about the process of knowing and how knowledge is acquired); each stage is characterized by a more complex and effective form of justification 19

Prereflective Reasoning (Stages 1-3): Belief that "knowledge is gained through the word of an authority figure or through firsthand observation, rather than, for example, through the evaluation of evidence. 20 believe that what they know is absolutely correct, and that they know with complete certainty. People who hold these assumptions treat all problems as though they were well-structured" (King & Kitchener, 2002, p. 39).

Quasi-Reflective Reasoning (Stages 4 and 5): Recognition "that knowledge-or more accurately, knowledge claims-contain elements of uncertainty, which 20 attribute to missing information or to methods of obtaining the evidence. Although they use evidence, they do not understand how evidence entails a conclusion (especially in light of the acknowledged uncertainty), and thus tend to view judgments as highly idiosyncratic" (King and Kitchener, 2002, p. 40).

Reflective Reasoning (Stages 6 and 7): People who hold these assumptions accept "that knowledge claims cannot be made with certainty, but [they] are not immobilized by it; rather, [they] make judgments that are "most reasonable" and about which they are "relatively certain," based on their evaluation of available data. They believe they must actively construct their decisions, and that knowledge claims must be evaluated in relationship to the context in which they were generated to determine their validity. They also readily admit their willingness to reevaluate the adequacy of their judgments as new data or new methodologies become available" (King & Kitchener, 2002, p. 40).

Epistemic vs aleatoric uncertainty

Epistemic uncertainty arises from a lack of knowledge or information about the true state of the world or the parameters of a generative model.

Aleatoric uncertainty stems from inherent, irreducible randomness or stochasticity in the environment.

This distinction has clear behavioral consequences. When faced with what they perceive as epistemic uncertainty, people are more likely to seek information and make more extreme probability judgments (i.e., closer to 0 or 1). In contrast, when uncertainty is perceived as aleatoric, they are more likely to make regressive judgments and adopt strategies like diversification to mitigate the inherent randomness

Continual learning is present from conception

Adult plasticity

Continual learning is made possible by the brain’s remarkable neuroplasticity - its ability to rewire and change in response to experience. While certain forms of plasticity are especially pronounced during early development (e.g. critical periods for language or vision), a variety of plasticity mechanisms operate throughout the entire lifespan.

For example, learning novel skills can induce measurable changes in brain structure and connectivity. In one classic study, adults who learned to juggle for just a few weeks showed transient increases in gray matter volume in brain areas related to visual-motion processing, demonstrating training-induced structural change in the adult brain. Similarly, an Oxford study found that adults training on a new complex skill (juggling) developed stronger white-matter connections in motor areas, highlighting that even beyond childhood the brain can rewire itself with practice.

Importantly, humans continue to learn and refine their internal world model across the entire lifespan, though the nature and efficiency of learning can change with age. During childhood and adolescence, plasticity is at its peak and foundational world knowledge (e.g. basic physics, language, social rules) is acquired at a rapid pace.

Certain learning abilities (often linked to fluid intelligence, like fast problem-solving or memorization of arbitrary patterns) tend to be strongest in youth and may gradually decline in later adulthood. However, other capacities - especially those involving accumulated knowledge and experience (crystallized intelligence) - actually increase or remain stable well into middle and older age. Adults continue to expand their knowledge base, vocabulary, and expertise over time, enriching their world model. Longitudinal studies show that middle-aged adults often perform better than they did as young adults on knowledge-based or skill-based tasks; for instance, verbal abilities, general knowledge, and inductive reasoning can improve up until the 50s or 60s. This means that even as raw learning speed or memory recall might slow down slightly, the breadth and depth of understanding of the world keeps growing for much of the lifespan.

In late adulthood, neuroplasticity is somewhat reduced compared to youth, but significant learning is still possible. The adage "you can’t teach an old dog new tricks" is misleading - older brains can and do learn, albeit sometimes more slowly. Studies have found that with practice and the right strategies, older individuals can acquire new skills nearly as well as younger people. For example, in one experiment older pilots took longer to learn how to use a flight simulator (slower initial learning), but ultimately they outperformed younger pilots at avoiding collisions, indicating that experience and accumulated knowledge gave them an edge in performance. Likewise, cognitive training research and real-world observations report that seniors can learn new languages, musical instruments, or technologies; while they may need more repetition, they often leverage their rich contextual knowledge to integrate the new information effectively. In fact, maintaining attentional focus and effective learning strategies can largely offset age-related slowing - one study noted that "if older people have really good attentive abilities they can learn as fast as younger people".

Thus, the extent of continual learning in humans is considerable: from infancy through old age, the human brain keeps adapting. The learning process becomes more about integrating new information with a vast store of prior knowledge (hence the wisdom of age), rather than the rapid unstructured acquisition seen in childhood. Crucially, even though the rate or style of learning changes, there is no point in the normal aging process at which the brain completely loses the capacity to form new memories or update its world model.

Neural Underpinnings

Nonnegativity and energetic efficiency drives modularity (along with data distribution) 29

Active dendrites

Sparse activations and updates

Cortical circuits maintain extremely sparse activity - only 1-5% of neurons fire above baseline at any moment. This sparsity serves multiple functions for continual learning.

First, it minimizes overlap between memory representations, reducing interference

Second, it creates a vast representational capacity - with 86 billion neurons, even 1% activity allows for essentially unlimited distinct patterns

Third, sparse coding is metabolically efficient, crucial given the brain’s 20W power budget. Layer 2/3 pyramidal cells in cortex show the sparsest activity (<0.5% active), implementing pattern separation

Mathematical analysis reveals sparse representations degrade gracefully - losing random neurons has minimal impact until >90% are removed, providing robustness against cellular turnover.

Continual turnover of inhibitory interneuron gain modulates this sparsity on demand, dynamically allocating unused coding space as experience accumulates.

The adult neurogenesis controversy remains unresolved, with conflicting high-profile studies showing either robust neurogenesis continuation or virtual absence in adult humans; however, there is evidence that, in the hippocampus, the dentate gyrus generates  700 new neurons daily in adult humans, with 3-7% annual turnover and enhanced plasticity for 4-6 weeks after birth, with 5x higher LTP amplitude and lower activation thresholds. New neurons preferentially encode recent experiences while mature neurons maintain remote memories, simultaneously expanding the space of possible encodings and allocating new memories to newly-formed subspaces (instead of overwriting existing subspaces).

Pressure on energetic efficiency may incentivize disentangled/sparse representations 30

Local learning rules

Use of local learning rules fundamentally prevents interference

The brain’s fundamental computation relies on purely local information-neurons update their synapses based only on pre- and postsynaptic activity plus diffusible neuromodulators, with no access to global error signals or network-wide gradients. This locality constraint, which seems limiting from a machine learning perspective, actually enables the brain’s remarkable continual learning capabilities by ensuring that learning in one circuit can’t accidentally corrupt distant, unrelated memories.

Synapse-specific three-factor STDP: Throughout cortex, striatum and cerebellum, weight updates obey a "pre x post x modulatory" rule: millisecond-scale spike-timing coincidence (pre x post) gates an eligibility trace that persists for  1-2 s, and a third, slower factor (e.g. dopamine, acetylcholine, norepinephrine) converts the trace into a lasting change. Because the eligibility trace is local to the synapse, only connections that actually participated in the recent computation are modified, sharply limiting interference with established circuitry. In striatum, phasic dopamine bursts amplify LTP 3-5 x on D1-expressing spines while depressing D2 spines, providing a signed credit-assignment signal that is both spatially confined (∼10 µm) and behaviour-contingent.

Branch-specific plasticity in pyramidal neurons. A single layer-5 pyramidal cell contains  20 semi-independent basal and apical dendritic compartments. NMDA or Ca2+ plateau potentials confined to one branch can induce LTP on clustered inputs while leaving neighbouring branches unchanged; heterosynaptic depression on adjacent, inactive spines prevents run-away excitation. Imaging studies show that when mice learn a new texture-discrimination task, <15% of branches in barrel cortex undergo structural enlargement, concentrating the memory trace in a tiny fraction of the neuronal substrate. This "dendritic modularity" allows a single neuron to store dozens of non-interfering associations across its lifetime.

Modularity across scales

Mesoscale graph structure. Tract-tracing and diffusion MRI reveal that mammalian cortex is a small-world, modular graph with within-module connection density 0.6-0.8 and between-module density 0.1-0.3; the Newmann-Girvan modularity coefficient Q 0.55. Motor-skill learning in humans increases intra-motor-module connectivity by  20% while leaving inter-module links statistically unchanged (<3% drift), demonstrating experience-dependent specialization that preserves global integration. Modular architectures with Newman’s modularity Q > 0.3 demonstrate enhanced robustness and flexible learning through functional specialization with no loss of integration.

Subcortical loop tiling. Basal-ganglia-thalamocortical loops are organised into at least 50 parallel "channels" (motor, oculomotor, dorsolateral prefrontal, limbic, etc.), each receiving topographically precise cortical input and projecting back to the originating area. Dopamine neurons project in variegated "striosome" versus "matrix" patterns, allowing reinforcement signals to be broadcast module-selectively. Likewise, the cerebellum is partitioned into  1000 micro-complexes, each <1 mm³, supporting fine-grained adaptive control without cross-talk.

Dynamic gating of modules. VIP->SST disinhibitory motifs act as local switches: when top-down or neuromodulatory input activates VIP cells, they silence SST interneurons, transiently lifting inhibition on a selected micro-column. Functional MRI shows that a burst of basal-forebrain acetylcholine can reconfigure large-scale modular boundaries within 200 ms, routing the same sensory stream through different cortical subnetworks depending on task context.

Pressure on energetic efficiency may incentivize disentangled/sparse representations 30

Multi-stage synaptic consolidation

The brain’s memory system operates like a distributed database with delayed commits and importance sampling. When pre- and postsynaptic neurons fire together, they don’t immediately strengthen their connection-instead, they generate temporary molecular tags through calcium-triggered phosphorylation cascades. These tags, primarily consisting of phosphorylated CaMKII and CREB, persist for approximately 60-120 minutes before degrading. During this window, the synapse enters a privileged state where it can capture plasticity-related proteins if they become available.

The decision to synthesize these proteins occurs at a higher level through neuromodulatory broadcast signals. When dopaminergic neurons in the ventral tegmental area detect reward prediction error, they fire phasic bursts at 15-20 Hz, releasing dopamine that diffuses across cubic millimeters of tissue. Similarly, the locus coeruleus noradrenergic system responds to novelty with firing rates jumping from 1-2 Hz baseline to 8-10 Hz, while basal forebrain cholinergic neurons modulate between 3-5 Hz during quiet states and 8-15 Hz during active attention. These neuromodulators trigger cAMP/PKA cascades that initiate protein synthesis, but only tagged synapses can capture and utilize these proteins for structural consolidation.

The acetylcholine system implements a particularly elegant state machine. During active waking, acetylcholine concentrations rise 200-300% above baseline, suppressing recurrent excitation in layer 2/3 pyramidal cells by activating presynaptic muscarinic receptors. This reduces interference between stored patterns and incoming sensory data-essentially implementing separate forward passes for encoding. When acetylcholine drops during quiet rest or slow-wave sleep, recurrent connections strengthen by 150-200%, enabling replay-driven consolidation. This temporal segregation means new memories can be encoded without corrupting existing ones, then selectively consolidated based on their behavioral relevance.

The synaptic redistribution hypothesis adds a critical constraint: neurons maintain total synaptic weight homeostasis through competitive dynamics. When dopamine-marked synapses strengthen through protein-synthesis-dependent consolidation, they literally steal AMPA receptors and postsynaptic density proteins from unmarked synapses. Experiments show this redistribution occurs with a time constant of 8-12 hours, implementing a soft memory capacity limit. The engineering brilliance is that important memories don’t just persist-they actively cannibalize resources from unimportant ones, creating automatic garbage collection without any centralized memory manager.

Synaptic metaplasticity

Every synapse has its own learning rate, set by X

Metaplasticity controls the plasticity induction threshold itself, determining whether stimulation can even generate tags in the first place. The BCM sliding threshold (θm) adjusts based on postsynaptic activity history: synapses that recently underwent LTP shift their threshold upward by 200-400%, while quiescent synapses gradually lower their threshold with a decay constant of 2-5 days. This creates a fundamental difference from tag-and-capture-metaplasticity prevents spurious plasticity at the source, while tag-and-capture filters which induced changes deserve consolidation.

The molecular implementation leverages overlapping mechanisms operating at distinct timescales. CaMKII autophosphorylation at threonine-286 creates a molecular memory lasting 10-100 minutes where the kinase remains partially active, biasing calcium sensing toward LTD. NMDA receptor subunit composition shifts from GluN2B (300ms calcium transients) to GluN2A (100ms transients) over 3-7 days following repeated activation, reducing calcium influx by 40-60%. SK2 potassium channels increase their membrane density by 150-200% after LTP, hyperpolarizing spines and requiring stronger depolarization for future plasticity. These mechanisms stack multiplicatively-a recently potentiated synapse might require 3-5x normal stimulation to generate new plasticity tags.

State-dependent modulation adds another control layer. During high cholinergic states, phosphorylation of SK2 channels reduces their conductance by 70%, effectively lowering θm across the network and making even "protected" synapses more plastic. Conversely, during slow-wave sleep, reduced neuromodulator tone allows local metaplastic history to dominate-frequently used synapses become nearly frozen while unused synapses remain available for recruitment. Quantitatively, the plasticity threshold can vary over a 10-fold range between the most protected and most available synapses within a single neuron.

The computational elegance emerges from the interaction between metaplasticity and consolidation. A well-consolidated synapse has elevated θm, preventing it from generating tags during routine activity. Only exceptional circumstances-synchronized volleys producing 50-100mV EPSPs or extreme stress triggering massive noradrenaline release-can overcome this barrier. Meanwhile, synapses that haven’t been used for several days return to baseline θm, ready to encode new information. This creates an implicit credit assignment system: the brain assumes frequently used synapses contain important information worth protecting, while dormant synapses represent available capacity. The protection isn’t absolute but probabilistic, with the threshold elevation implementing a soft exponential decay of plasticity probability as a function of recent use-essentially online elastic weight consolidation without explicit importance weights.

Structural Constraints on Plasticity

Adult plasticity operates within tight structural bounds that prevent runaway changes. While synaptic weights can change rapidly (minutes), creating new synapses requires hours to days, and establishing new long-range connections takes weeks to months.

Axonal boutons show 7% monthly turnover, while dendritic spines turn over at 5-15% depending on cortical area. This structural inertia implements an implicit regularization - rapid learning affects only existing connections while slower structural changes require sustained experience.

The extracellular matrix, particularly perineuronal nets around inhibitory neurons, further restricts plasticity after critical periods. Once in place, these nets restrict spine motility, clamp intracellular chloride levels, and dampen calcium influx, all of which raise the local plasticity threshold and effectively "freeze" the surrounding microcircuit. Circuits that underwrite core skills-orientation maps in V1, song syllables in zebra finches, well-practiced motor sequences-tend to become PNN-stabilized, protecting them from later experience.

These structural constraints follow a curriculum, which should be central to this section

Complementary learning systems

The computational trade-off at the heart of the CLS framework is between learning the specific details of individual experiences and extracting the general statistical structure that holds across many experiences. An agent must be able to remember where it parked its car today (a specific, one-off episode) and also learn the best general strategy for finding a parking spot (a statistical regularity). These two learning objectives are computationally antagonistic. Learning specifics requires rapid synaptic changes and representations that are highly separated to prevent interference between similar memories (e.g., today’s parking spot vs. yesterday’s). In contrast, learning generalities requires slow, incremental synaptic changes and overlapping representations that allow the system to discover shared structure across many different events.

The brain’s architectural solution is to assign these conflicting tasks to two anatomically distinct and computationally complementary systems: the hippocampus and the neocortex. The hippocampus serves as a rapid learning system, encoding specific episodes within minutes using sparse, pattern-separated representations. Its dentate gyrus performs pattern separation with an expansion ratio of 5:1 (from 200,000 entorhinal inputs to 1 million granule cells), ensuring new memories don’t overwrite old ones. Meanwhile, the neocortex implements slow learning over months to years, gradually extracting statistical regularities through interleaved hippocampal replay. This division of labor allows rapid adaptation without disrupting consolidated knowledge - new information enters through the hippocampus and transfers to cortex only after extensive replay and abstraction.

Memory transfer from hippocampus to neocortex follows precise spatiotemporal dynamics. During quiet waking and NREM sleep, sharp-wave ripples (150-250 Hz oscillations lasting 50-150ms) in hippocampus coincide with cortical slow oscillations (0.5-4 Hz) and sleep spindles (12-15 Hz). Each ripple replays compressed sequences at 10-20x real-time speed, with place cell sequences maintaining their temporal order but compressed from seconds to milliseconds.

Critically, this isn’t simple repetition - each replay occurs in a different cortical context, enabling abstraction. The process continues for weeks to months, with memories becoming progressively more cortical and less hippocampal-dependent. This process is known to actively stabilize and reorganize memories, allowing new information to be integrated without overwriting old knowledge. By reactivating and stabilizing both new and old memories, sleep enables continual learning, allowing the knowledge base to expand without succumbing to interference

Development of the episodic memory system is crucial for CLS-supported continual learning

As a sidenote, an interesting way to view the architectural specialization of the PFC and HPC is to view as modules that respectively store memories in their firing patterns and in their weights at inference-time 31; this further corresponds to the tension between flexibility/generalization and high-fidelity storage

Cognitive Underpinnings

Sensorimotor grounding

Sensorimotor grounding provides the foundational architecture for continual learning by establishing a stable hierarchy of reusable representations that emerge from the fundamental constraints of embodied interaction with the physical world. Unlike abstract symbolic representations that can vary arbitrarily across domains, sensorimotor primitives are constrained by the physics of the environment and the biomechanics of the body, creating natural invariances that persist across learning contexts. When an infant learns to reach for objects, they’re not just acquiring a specific motor skill-they’re building low-level representations of spatial relationships, force dynamics, and temporal sequences that become the building blocks for virtually every future manipulation task.

The genius of this system lies in how physical embodiment naturally creates a compositional representational hierarchy. Low-level sensorimotor primitives like edge detection, motion parallax, and basic force vectors remain remarkably stable because they reflect fundamental properties of physics that don’t change across domains. Mid-level representations-such as object affordances, spatial navigation primitives (e.g entorhinal grid and border cells), and basic action schemas-emerge from combinations of these low-level features but inherit their stability. This creates what’s essentially a universal coordinate system for experience: when you learn to use a new tool, you’re not learning entirely new representations but rather new compositions of existing sensorimotor primitives for grasping, applying force, and coordinating visual feedback. Besides increasing learning speed, the presence of highly transferable low- and mid-level representations implies that minimal modifications need to be made to the brain to accommadate new information, minimizing the risk of interference.

Schematic scaffolding

Schematic knowledge acts as the cognitive backbone that allows biological brains to continuously acquire new information without catastrophic forgetting. When you learn that San Francisco has approximately 815,000 residents and 49 square miles of land area, you don’t need to relearn what a city is, what population means, or how geographic measurements work. Your existing schemas about cities, demographics, and geography provide the scaffolding that makes this new learning incredibly efficient.

The power of schemas becomes quantitatively apparent in memory studies. Research shows that chess masters can reconstruct board positions with 93% accuracy after viewing them for just 5 seconds, while novices achieve only 20% accuracy. This isn’t due to superior visual memory - when pieces are arranged randomly rather than in game-realistic positions, experts perform no better than novices. The experts’ chess schemas allow them to chunk information into meaningful patterns, reducing cognitive load from remembering 20-30 individual piece positions to remembering 5-7 meaningful configurations.

This scaffolding effect operates through multiple mechanisms. First, schemas provide attentional templates that guide what information gets encoded. Eye-tracking studies reveal that experts spend 70% more time fixating on diagnostically relevant features compared to novices when learning new domain-specific information. Second, schemas enable predictive coding - the brain can allocate its limited learning capacity to prediction errors rather than redundantly encoding predictable information. Neuroimaging shows that schema-consistent information activates the medial prefrontal cortex and shows rapid consolidation (within 24 hours), while schema-inconsistent information requires the hippocampus and takes weeks to consolidate.

The engineering principle here is profound: biological brains achieve continual learning not by preventing forgetting, but by building hierarchical knowledge structures that minimize what needs to be learned in the first place. When a child learns about elephants after already knowing about dogs and cats, they’re not learning an entirely new concept but rather learning the delta - the specific deviations from their existing mammal schema. This compression ratio can be dramatic; studies suggest that schema-based encoding can reduce the information content of new memories by 10-40x while maintaining equivalent behavioral performance.

Perhaps most remarkably, schemas don’t just facilitate learning of consistent information - they also enhance memory for schema-inconsistent information through the "schema-copy-plus-tag" mechanism. The brain appears to store both the expected schema-based representation and explicitly tag the violations, which explains why we remember unusual events (like seeing a penguin in a desert) particularly well. This dual-coding strategy allows biological systems to maintain stable world models while remaining sensitive to novel information that could signal important environmental changes.

The Scaffolding Theory of Aging and Cognition (STAC) argues that accumulated schemas enable older adults to compensate for neural decline: they rely more heavily on prefrontal "scaffold" networks that leverage well-honed knowledge structures, preserving performance despite slower hippocampal encoding. This supports a continuum view of continual learning in which schematic depth, not just raw synaptic plasticity, underwrites adaptability. Educational studies in children likewise show that rich domain knowledge predicts future learning rates better than working-memory span-schematic slots matter more than sheer capacity.

Schematic scaffolding suggests that effective world models should:

Learn hierarchical, generative scripts that span from sensorimotor routines to abstract event graphs, enabling zero-shot inference when new experiences slot into known structures.

Maintain novelty-sensitive gating-preferentially invoking hippocampal-like episodic modules only when prediction errors exceed schema tolerance.

Use replay or self-supervised reinstatement to integrate schema-consistent experiences into long-term stores without exhaustive rehearsal.

Exploit meta-learning objectives that encourage formation of transferable schemas rather than over-fitting to task-specific surface statistics.

Metacognition

Metacognitive mechanisms, centered in rostrolateral prefrontal cortex, enable performance monitoring, strategy selection, and learning rate modulation. At its core, metacognition enables humans to monitor their own learning processes and strategically allocate cognitive resources based on confidence estimates and uncertainty signals. This creates a remarkably efficient learning system where humans spend roughly 80% of their study time on material they’re least confident about, compared to random allocation strategies that show no such bias.

The key engineering principle here is that metacognitive monitoring acts as a built-in curriculum generator. When humans encounter new information, their metacognitive systems continuously estimate learning progress through confidence judgments and feeling-of-knowing assessments. This creates dynamic difficulty adjustment in real-time - if confidence drops below threshold levels, attention and rehearsal resources are automatically redirected. Studies show that people with better metacognitive calibration (correlation between confidence and actual performance) demonstrate 40-60% faster learning rates across domains, suggesting this monitoring system provides genuine computational advantages rather than mere subjective experience.

Perhaps most critically for continual learning, metacognition enables strategic forgetting and interference management. The brain doesn’t just passively accumulate information - it actively decides what deserves consolidation into long-term memory based on metacognitive assessments of relevance and retrieval success.
